**Surah al-Fil (The Elephant)**

Its purpose is to show the destruction of those who amass wealth, in the abode of mutual support and aid through means. When those means are cut off, the destruction is all the more fitting, because Allah, glory be to Him, alone possesses complete power, not one who is empowered by wealth and men. Its name, al-Fil (the Elephant), clearly indicates this when one reflects on its surah and on what happened to the army and its form. [The surah opens with] "In the name of Allah" (*bismillah*), whose encompassing power acts in everything; "the Most Gracious" (*al-Rahman*), who possesses all-embracing blessing; and "the Most Merciful" (*al-Rahim*), who specially grants complete blessing to the people of election.

* *

When the previous surah (al-Humazah) stated that the abundance of wealth which brings about strength through men may lead to ruin, this surah demonstrates it with an evident proof that reached [the people] in its burning and penetration into bodies and its scraping into hearts, in the lesser punishment, as the earlier surah mentioned the greater, hidden punishment. It warns against prominence in this world and high rank, indicating that the more greatly they are magnified, the more harm they cause, through the rebellion they produce, until their possessor contends with the Supreme King. Although this is evident, the Arabs, and Quraysh in particular, have complete knowledge of it. So [Allah] said, affirming and rebuking those who entertain any contrary notion:

﴿Have you not seen?﴾ That is, do you know with a knowledge which, in its certainty, is like the sensible presence seen by the eye. This is because the Prophet ﷺ, although he did not witness that event, did witness its traces, heard its reports through widespread transmission, and Allah informed him of its details. He ﷺ was singled out [in the address] to inform that this is known and acted upon only by him ﷺ and those whom Allah enables to follow him well, because of the human being's ties to deficiency and to the pulls of desire and forgetfulness. It is read as "*tar*" with the *ra'* sukun (*lam tar*), which the grammarians say is for the sake of showing the effect of the jussive particle. The secret of this reading is an indication urging speed in seeing, implying that their matter, despite their large number, was like the blink of an eye. Whoever does not attend to it and hasten to deliberately contemplate it will not grasp it as it should be grasped.

Since the one who considers the manner [of this event] must look carefully and verify the aspects of the indications of the perfection of Allah's knowledge and power, and of the honouring of His Prophet through a foreshadowing sign (*irhas*, a sign preceding prophethood) of his prophethood and the establishing of his mission, and of the magnifying of His city and the ennobling of his people, [Allah] said "*how*" (*kayfa*), rather than saying "what" (*ma*), [He] "*did*" (*fa'ala*), that is, the doing of one who has the most complete motive for that act. The verb of seeing is suspended from "how" because of the interrogative meaning it carries, so its governing verb cannot precede it; rather, its object is a verb suspended, and the interrogative clause is in the place of an accusative complement of the suspended verb. ﴿Your Lord⦆, that is, the One who has done good to you (*al-muhsin ilayk*), and from His goodness to your people, through you and through this extraordinary event, [He did it as] a foreshadowing sign of your prophethood, as is known from the reports of the earlier prophets concerning what occurs before their prophethoods of this kind, so that it would support their claim to prophethood afterward. In singling him out with the address, and in the mention of "Lord" together with honouring him, and in the reference through mentioning Him, there is an allusion to the lowliness of the idols which they named as lords. Whoever believes will know this from them with the knowledge of certainty; and whoever persists in disbelief will know it with the truth of certainty when Allah gives His Messenger ﷺ power over them in the Sacred City, and makes it lawful for him in the highest state and aim.

﴿With the People of the Elephant⦆, that is, those who intended to violate the sanctities of Allah, glory be to Him, so that they would ruin His House and tear apart its neighbours, by means of the wealth and strength with which Allah, glory be to Him, had favoured them, which led them to insolence. They reckoned that these would make them immortal, but it became clear that they were leading them to ruin, the opposite of what they had reckoned. They were the Abyssinians who had overcome the land of Yemen. Their commander, Abu Yaksum, Abraha ibn al-Sabah al-Ashram, built a church in San'a and named it al-Qalis, on the pattern of *Qabit*, and he wanted to divert to it, so he claimed, the pilgrimage of the Arabs. A man from Kinanah went and defecated in it at night, smearing it with it. This angered al-Ashram. He inquired, and it was said to him: "We think the perpetrator is from the people of the house in Makkah." He swore that he would demolish the Ka'bah. Among the wonders of Allah's craftsmanship is that He inspired him, glory be to Him, to name it by this name, which is derived from *al-qals*, one of whose meanings is water that comes out of the throat, filling the mouth, which is the origin of vomiting, the brother of defecation, to which its matter came. Thus it was the cause of its own destruction, through the destruction of its builder.

This is because he became angry at that and set out with his army to demolish the House of Allah, the Ka'bah, and with him were many elephants, among them a great elephant named Mahmud. Some of the Arabs fought him, and he defeated them and killed some of them. When he subdued them, they submitted to him. When he reached al-Mughammas, Abd al-Muttalib, grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ, went out to him, and offered him a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he turn back from them. It was also said: his advance guard had seized for him two hundred camels, and he demanded them from him. He said: "I was impressed by you when I saw you, but I lost interest in you when you speak to me about two hundred camels and leave aside speaking to me about a house which is your religion and your honour?" He said: "You and that." So he returned his camels to him, and he drove them off and went on. He ordered Quraysh to disperse into the ravines and take refuge in the mountains. Abd al-Muttalib came to the Ka'bah, took hold of the ring of the door, and began to say:

*O Lord, I hope for none but You for them,*
*So keep them from approaching Your sanctuary.*

And he said:

*O God, a man defends his household,*
*So defend Your sacred ground.*

*Let not their cross and their might*
*Overcome Your might, O Foe of Yours.*

*If You leave them and our Ka'bah,*
*Then decide as You see fit.*

Then he let go of the ring and went off towards some of those directions. When morning came, Abraha prepared to enter the Sacred Precinct, and arrayed his army, and the elephant came forward and knelt down. They tried to make it rise, but no stratagem was effective with it. They turned it towards other than the Sacred Precinct, and it began to run; they turned it towards the Sacred Precinct, and it knelt down. This was its practice on that day. While they were in that state, Allah, exalted be He, sent against them birds in flocks (*ababil*), each bird carrying in its beak a pebble and in its two feet two pebbles, each pebble larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea. They pelted them with these, and the pebble would fall on a man's head and come out through his posterior, and they all perished. The people of Makkah and the Arabs present on the mountain tops were watching Allah's handiwork against them and His goodness towards them, that is, the people of Makkah. This was a foreshadowing sign of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, for it occurred in the year of his birth. Hamzah al-Karmani said: "In another report: on the day of his birth." It seems it was a cause of their weakness, until Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan went to Khosrow and brought back from him an army which uprooted their remnant, as is well known in the biographies and transmitted in the reports. Quraysh sent a delegation to congratulate him on victory over them, and their leader was Abd al-Muttalib, grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ. Sayf gave him good news that a son would be born to him named Muhammad. He informed him that a son had been born to him and that his father had died. Sayf told him that he was the Prophet who would be sent at the end of time, that Yathrib would be his place of emigration, and that had he known he would live until the time of his mission, he would have gone to Yathrib and made it his dwelling until he would help the Prophet ﷺ there and make his prophethood manifest.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surah al-Humazah included the mention of the deception of the one who is seduced by his wealth, to the point that he thinks it will make him immortal, and what that led to, he followed this with the People of the Elephant, whom their numbers had deceived, and whom their spread through the lands and their domination had tricked, until they resolved to demolish the Sacred House. So they hastened to their retribution. Allah made their scheme go astray, and sent against them birds in flocks, that is, scattered groups, pelting them with stones of *sijjil*, until they uprooted them and cut off their last trace, and made them like chewed-up straw. That deception of theirs, through the abundance of their share of the loss mentioned earlier, produced this result. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 105, verse 2:

When he had established it by the manner (of the event), as a reminder of the aspects of indication within it concerning the preliminaries of the message (al-risalah), he pointed to those aspects, placing before them another affirmation that comprehends their story and informs of their distress, so he said: ﴿Did He not make their plan﴾, that is, by what He has of benevolence toward the Arabs, especially the Quraysh, ﴿their plan﴾ [that is -] in nullifying the Ka'bah by demolishing it and diverting the pilgrimage to their church according to their claim, and [indeed -] their plan was great, by which they overcame whoever opposed them among the Arabs, ﴿into misguidance﴾, that is, enclosed and lost in what they aimed at of abrogating the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah first and demolishing it second, and in nullification, straying from rectitude, and neglect, such that by being enclosed in that, and filled with it, it has no escape from it. This indicates that whoever meddles with anything of the sacred things of Allah, such as one of His houses or one of His friends (awliya') or one of the scholars of the religion, even if he is somewhat deficient, falls into His scheme, and the evil of his wickedness returns upon him: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war upon him." It also indicates that whoever openly commits disobedience, destruction hastens to him, unlike the one who conceals it. And it indicates that Allah the Exalted comes upon whoever He wills to punish from where he does not reckon, so that caution against Him endures and His scheme is not deemed safe, even if the adversary is the least of His servants. The Abyssinians had not imagined what befell them at all, nor did it occur to anyone other than them that birds would kill an army that subdued champions and to which the mightiest men submitted, led by a mighty king whose battalion walks in the plain and whose foot is upon the hurling stones at the tops of the mountain passes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 105, verse 3:

Since the implied sense is: "He prevented them from entering the sanctuary of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, let alone from reaching the city of the Messenger ﷺ," the phrase is coordinated (ʿaṭf) either with that sense or with "yajʿalu" (﴿He makes﴾). It is stated in the past tense because it carries the meaning of the past, which is clearer, and expressing it in the past is more firmly established. His words ﴿And He sent﴾ are clarified as sending a punishment by His words ﴿upon them﴾, meaning specifically from among those disbelievers of the Arabs who were there. This indicates their humiliation and debasement, that He would punish them with something not great, because they magnified themselves and acted arrogantly toward their Creator through the ugly intention toward His House. So the Exalted said, informing that He sent against them what [lā -] would not kill its like in the ordinary course: ﴿birds﴾. It is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) that is masculine in its wording and feminine in meaning, and it may also apply to a single bird. For this reason He said, clarifying the abundance, ﴿in flocks﴾, meaning very many groups, scattered, following one another from various directions, company after company and troop after troop, with a bird in front of each group leading it, red of beak, black of head, and long of neck. Abu ʿUbayda said: It is said, "Horses came in flocks (abābīl) from here and from there." It is the plural of ibbāla (with a kasra and shadda), which is a large bundle, and the group of birds was likened to it in their being packed together. In their proverbs: "ḍaghth ʿalā ibbāla," meaning one calamity upon another.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 105, verse 4:

When the listener was eager to know what the birds did to them, He said, beginning a new statement: ﴿They pelted them﴾, that is, the birds, ﴿with stones﴾, that is, great in number and effect, but small in size and volume; each one of them was about the size of a lentil (ʿadasa), one in the beak of each bird and one in each of its feet.

When a thing is made for punishment, it is more severe in its effect upon the one it strikes, He said: ﴿of baked clay﴾, that is, of hardened clay, made for punishment, [cast] from a place at the highest elevation, as explained in Surah Hud (upon him be prayers and peace). Hamza al-Karmani said: Abu Salih said: "I saw those stones streaked with red."

When their destruction resulted from this throwing, and that was by the action of Allah, glorified and exalted, the One capable of what He wills, because He is the One who created the effect, decisively, since the like of it does not produce what resulted of destruction, He said: ﴿So He made them﴾, i.e., your Lord, who is good to you by His goodness to (p. 258) your people for your sake, through that, ﴿like chewed-up husks﴾, i.e., the leaves of a crop upon which the eater has fallen, which is that worms eat it and hollow it out. This is because the stone would come down on the head and pierce through, by its heat and the intensity of its impact, everything it passed through until it exits from the rear, and the place of its hollowing becomes black because of its fiery nature. Or [it is like] a grain eaten so that it remained empty of its contents, or like chaff that animals ate and voided. But it came in the manner of the etiquette of the Qur'an, like His saying, exalted: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 75]. And this destruction, in its wonder, is among the meanings of the rhetorical interrogative (istifham taqriri) at its beginning, so its two ends embrace and its last wraps around its first. And Allah knows best His intent.
